content: 1. Bedaquiline is primarily metabolized by the enzyme CYP3A4. When used concurrently with efavirenz (EFV) or protease inhibitors (PIs), there is a potential for significant alterations in drug concentrations. This necessitates extreme caution and close clinical monitoring. Alternative antiretroviral (ARV) options should be considered in such cases. 2. When using ARV drugs alongside direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) for hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, potential drug interactions must be carefully evaluated. Simeprevir and the combination of ombitasvir, paritaprevir, ritonavir, and dasabuvir should not be co-administered with any protease inhibitors (PIs) or non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs). 3. Daclatasvir has significant drug interactions with many NNRTIs and PIs. Its concurrent use requires careful consideration, dose adjustments, or the selection of alternative DAAs. 4. Ledipasvir and sofosbuvir exhibit a reduced potential for drug interactions with ARV drugs due to their reliance on different metabolic pathways. 5. Although access to DAAs remains limited in many regions, ribavirin and pegylated interferon alpha-2a are being used less frequently for HCV treatment. Co-administration of these agents with zidovudine (AZT) has been associated with an increased risk of anemia and hepatic decompensation. 6. Antifungal agents such as itraconazole and ketoconazole are commonly used to treat fungal infections. However, nevirapine (NVP) may reduce their concentrations to subtherapeutic levels. Alternative antifungal agents, such as flucytosine and fluconazole, should be considered to ensure effective treatment in individuals with HIV. 7. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends artemisinin-based combination therapies for treating uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria. One such combination, artesunate and amodiaquine, is associated with increased amodiaquine concentrations when used with efavirenz (EFV), leading to a significant rise in liver transaminases. Halofantrine and lumefantrine should not be used with PIs. Alternative artemisinin-based therapies, such as artesunate plus mefloquine or artesunate plus sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, may be safer options for individuals with HIV. 8. For opioid substitution therapy, WHO recommends methadone and buprenorphine for managing opioid dependence. Co-administration of efavirenz (EFV) reduces methadone concentrations, potentially causing withdrawal symptoms and increasing the risk of relapse. Individuals on methadone and NNRTIs should be closely monitored, and methadone doses may need adjustment. 9. ARV drugs can alter the levels of steroid hormones in hormonal contraceptives, either increasing or decreasing their concentrations. Interactions between some NNRTIs and ritonavir-boosted PIs with hormonal contraceptives may reduce the effectiveness of both the contraceptive and the ARV drug. Injectable formulations of depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) are unaffected by ARV drugs and can be used without restriction. However, long-acting progestogen-only implants may have reduced efficacy when used with efavirenz (EFV). Women on ART who choose hormonal contraceptives should also use condoms and other contraceptive methods to prevent both HIV transmission and unintended pregnancies. 10. Concomitant use of boosted PIs and NNRTIs with certain antihistamines, such as astemizole and terfenadine, has been linked to severe and life-threatening reactions, including cardiac arrhythmias. Safer alternatives include loratadine and cetirizine. 11. WHO recommends statins for individuals with a 10-year cardiovascular risk exceeding 30%. Boosted PIs can increase the concentrations of lovastatin and simvastatin, raising the risk of serious adverse events such as myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Alternative cholesterol-lowering agents should be used to avoid severe toxicity in individuals with HIV. 12. Dolutegravir (DTG) should not be administered simultaneously with cation-containing antacids, laxatives, or multivitamin/mineral supplements due to the risk of chelation. If combined, DTG should be taken at least two hours before or six hours after medications containing polyvalent cations. 13. Zidovudine (AZT) should be substituted with tenofovir (TDF) when co-administered with ribavirin and pegylated interferon alpha-2a due to the increased risk of anemia and hepatic decompensation. 14. Rifampicin should be replaced with rifabutin when used with boosted PIs to avoid significant drug interactions. Alternatively, the dose of lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) can be adjusted, or a regimen with three nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) can be used in children. 15. Halofantrine and lumefantrine should be avoided with PIs. Alternative antimalarial agents should be considered. 16. Lovastatin and simvastatin should be replaced with alternative cholesterol-lowering agents to prevent severe toxicity. 17. Hormonal contraceptives may require alternative or additional contraceptive methods to ensure efficacy when used with ARV drugs. 18. Methadone and buprenorphine doses should be adjusted as needed when co-administered with ARV drugs. 19. Astemizole and terfenadine should be replaced with alternative antihistamines to avoid severe reactions. 20. Dolutegravir (DTG) should be taken at least two hours before or six hours after supplements containing polyvalent cations to prevent chelation.
